whyItExists.problem: Programs need to store and reuse values — a user's name, a score, whether a checkbox is checked. Without variables, you would have to repeat every value everywhere.
whyItExists.solution: Variables are named storage containers. You declare them with let or const, give them a name, and assign a value. JavaScript has 8 data types covering all common values.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time you need to store, reuse, or change a value in your program.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Never use var in modern JavaScript — it has function scope and hoisting behaviour that causes bugs. Always use let or const.

explainModes.beginner: A variable is a labelled box. You write the label (name) and put something in the box (value). Later you can read from the box or change what's in it. const boxes cannot be changed after you fill them.
explainModes.simple: let declares a variable you can reassign. const declares one you cannot reassign. Use const by default; switch to let only when you need to reassign. JavaScript has 7 primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol — plus object.
explainModes.standard: JavaScript is dynamically typed — variables have no fixed type. The same variable can hold a string, then a number. typeof returns a string describing the type. Primitives are immutable values; objects are mutable references. undefined means 'declared but not assigned'; null means 'intentionally empty'.
explainModes.technical: Primitives are stored by value (copied on assignment). Objects are stored by reference (two variables can point to the same object). const prevents reassignment of the binding — not mutation of the object. Temporal Dead Zone: let/const bindings exist from the start of their block scope but cannot be accessed before the declaration line.
explainModes.deepDive: JavaScript numbers are IEEE 754 double-precision floats — there is only one number type. This causes 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3. For currency, use integer cents or a library like decimal.js. BigInt (suffix n: 9007199254740993n) handles integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. The Symbol type creates globally unique primitive values — used as non-string object property keys in library code.

content.code:
typeof 'hello'     // 'string'
typeof 42          // 'number'
typeof true        // 'boolean'
typeof undefined   // 'undefined'
typeof null        // 'object'  ← famous JS bug (null is NOT an object)
typeof {}          // 'object'
typeof []          // 'object'  ← arrays are objects
typeof function(){} // 'function'

content.text: typeof null returns 'object' — this is a long-standing JavaScript bug that cannot be fixed for backwards compatibility. To check for null: use value === null.

content.code:
// JavaScript automatically converts types in some operations
'5' + 3      // '53'  (number 3 converted to string)
'5' - 3      // 2     (string '5' converted to number)
'5' * '2'   // 10    (both converted to numbers)
Boolean(0)  // false
Boolean('')  // false
Boolean(null) // false
Boolean([]) // true   (empty array is truthy!)

// Use === (strict equality) to avoid coercion surprises
5 == '5'   // true  (loose — converts types)
5 === '5'  // false (strict — no conversion) ← always use this

content.text: Always use === and !== for comparisons. The loose equality operators (== and !=) perform type coercion that leads to surprising results.

content.title: Try it: Variables and types

questions.question: Which keyword should you use for a variable that will NOT be reassigned?
questions.explanation: const declares a variable that cannot be reassigned. Use const by default and switch to let only when you need to reassign the variable.

questions.question: What does 5 === '5' evaluate to?
questions.explanation: === is strict equality — it does NOT convert types. 5 is a number and '5' is a string, so they are not equal. Always use === to avoid unexpected type coercion.

questions.question: What does typeof null return?
questions.explanation: typeof null returns 'object' — a known JavaScript bug from 1995 that cannot be fixed without breaking existing code. To check for null specifically, use value === null.

faq.q: What is the difference between undefined and null?
faq.a: undefined means a variable was declared but never assigned a value — JavaScript sets this automatically. null means intentionally absent — you set this deliberately to indicate 'no value here'. Both are falsy.

faq.q: Can I change the type of a variable?
faq.a: Yes. JavaScript is dynamically typed — you can assign a string to a variable and later assign a number to the same variable. This is flexible but can lead to bugs; TypeScript adds static types to prevent this.

faq.q: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not exactly 0.3 in JavaScript?
faq.a: JavaScript uses IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic, which cannot represent all decimal fractions exactly in binary. 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004. For money, use integer cents (store 150 for £1.50) or a decimal library.
